tasks.title: Expose the .cnb content format
tasks.currentState: Done. 248 of the 272 routes are bound and reached, and the loader registry -- the one part that needed a decision rather than more binding -- is answered in docs/cnb-loader-registry-decision.md. Eight asset families read and write, five of them crossing to the XNA type a game uses. The model family is complete. CnbImport reads PNG, JPEG, WAV and DDS; Cnj compiles the .cnj documents that say what to do with them, reporting absorbed sources and external references for a build system. CnbLoaders dispatches a document to the loader that may read it, implementing CNA's identity rule rather than projecting its C-callback table.
tasks.expectedState: Achieved. What stays unbound is stated with its reason rather than left open: the loader registration and invoke routes need a C callback and return a void* no Java call could receive; cna_cnb_model_add_animation takes a nested descriptor graph the generator refuses rather than guesses at, so animations are read rather than written; and cna_cnb_texture_data_select_representation takes a predicate callback.
tasks.note: Every .cnb fixture is produced by CNA's own encoder and read back by CNA's own parser, so a successful read means the file is real. The importer and .cnj fixtures are deliberately the opposite -- a PNG written by the JDK, a WAV and a DDS and a BMP written from their published layouts, JSON written by the test -- because there the source format is what is under test and a CNA-authored input would prove nothing. The model family was probed in C first: tools/native-abi/probes/cnb_model_roundtrip.c.

tasks.title: Bind the native Model routes behind the managed XNB model graph
tasks.currentState: Done. The model extension routes are bound: cameras and skins are authored through CnaModel.addCamera and addSkin, a skin's skeleton comes back as its own CnaSkinningData, a bind pose is applied with applyBindPoseBoneTransforms, and a mesh part carries its own primitive type, per-slot sampler state and morph data. The reason recorded here -- that they are "read-useful only on a model CNA imported, which the blocked content loader is the way to get" -- was wrong about the direction: they are WRITE-useful on a model Java built, which CnaModel.From already produced.
tasks.expectedState: The XNA Model graph reaches CNA. CnaModel.From(Model) builds CNA's own model over the buffers and effects the XNA model already owns -- retained, not copied, so nothing is uploaded twice -- and CNA then draws it in one call and computes its bone transforms. models.h is fully classified: 184 extension candidates, 31 not useful in Java, and one deferred route, the loader JAVA-UPSTREAM-004 blocks.
tasks.note: Load<Model> deliberately stays on the managed XNB reader. XNB records the effect's type and the reader builds the BasicEffect an XNA game casts to; CNA publishes a loaded effect as a handle whose type is only a name, so routing the strict load through CNA would break (BasicEffect) part.getEffect(). The measurement is in CnaModelTests, which reads one authored .xnb through both runtimes and compares their graphs bone for bone.

tasks.title: Reach or unbind the 162 routes no Java call site touches

tasks.title: Three value types leaked the CNA handles they owned
tasks.currentState: Fixed, and it was three types rather than one. NetworkSessionProperties' public constructor, all four AvatarDescription paths, and every LeaderboardEntry created an owned CNA handle that nothing released; none of the three is IDisposable in XNA, so a game had nothing to close and no way to know. LeaderboardReader.getEntries was the worst: every entry CNA hands out is an owned copy, so the leak grew with each call of an ordinary getter. Measured: cna_network_session_properties_destroy answers CNA_RESULT_THREAD from any thread but the creating one, so a Cleaner could not release any of them either.
tasks.expectedState: org.openeggbert.cna.internal.NativeDeferredRelease records the handle when the Java object becomes unreachable and the owning thread releases it at the next FrameworkDispatcher.Update, which is where this binding already does deferred native work. A session-owned list registers nothing, because the session frees it.

tasks.title: Two gates could not see an ABI migration go wrong
tasks.currentState: Done. The generator keeps an unwind list of unconditional releases in acquisition order, and every early return replays it in reverse. It could not reuse the existing cleanup list, which is why this was recorded rather than fixed in passing: some of those statements are guarded on the call's result, which is not declared yet at the point an acquisition can fail.
tasks.expectedState: Every early return releases what it holds, and the success path still releases each acquisition exactly once. Three tool tests check both, on the four-array route that made the defect ordinary rather than rare.

The Guide slice projects the pending on-screen keyboard and message box, CNA's renderer for them, the outcomes a game reports back and the achievements pane (16 routes). The net slice answers where a session is and adds the direction XNA cannot reach at all -- describing a session at a known address so NetworkSession.Join can take it. The avatar slice projects the appearance colours a real-rendered avatar is drawn in, the clip an animation plays, and the clip and content names behind XNA's canonical presets and body types (9 routes).

And a discovered session carries the host and port it was found at, which AvailableNetworkSession does not name: 4 routes.

Exposing them with a raw long handle would be an API a game cannot safely use, and half of a two-step contract is worse than none. JAVA-EXT-007 finishes them.

tasks.title: Project CNA's skinned model, and finish real avatar rendering on top of it
tasks.currentState: Done. The blocker recorded here -- "cna_skinning_data_create takes a CNA_SkinningDataDescriptor, a pointer graph the generator refuses rather than guesses at, and no route takes a clip handle, so there is no other door in" -- was true in every clause and did not follow. A shape a generator cannot derive is not a lifetime nobody knows: CNA states every array as borrowed for the call and every descriptor as deeply copied, so three hand-written marshallers build the graphs for one call each, checking every count against every array first. CnaSkinningData, CnaAnimationPlayer, CnaSkinnedModel, CnaMorphTargetData, CnaModelAnimations, CnbClip.encode and CnbModelData.addAnimation are all built on them, and AvatarExtensions can now switch a renderer to a real model and draw a clip on it.

CnaSkinningData, CnaAnimationPlayer, CnaSkinnedModel, CnaMorphTargetData, CnaModelAnimations, CnbClip.encode and CnbModelData.addAnimation are all built on them, and AvatarExtensions can now switch a renderer to a real model and draw a clip on it.

tasks.title: Project CNA's engine layer, one family at a time
tasks.currentState: 844 of the engine layer 857 routes are bound and reached, up from 778. The sixty-six that moved were not waiting on Java: compute and storage buffers, automatic exposure, the light-probe baker three bake routes, the render pipeline two scene callbacks, and twenty-two lent handles, each of which needed a renderer or a measurement rather than more code. Every one of the thirteen still unbound has a written reason that is not a renderer.
tasks.expectedState: Done as far as this runtime can qualify it. 778 of the 857 routes are bound and reached, and each of the remaining 79 has a written reason rather than a plan: 27 are the compute family (JAVA-EXT-012), 13 automatic exposure (JAVA-EXT-011) and 20 lend a handle whose lifetime the declaration does not state or that comes back invalid here (JAVA-EXT-010), all three measured with a real graphics device. The other 19 are named individually -- nine texture getters that mint a fresh handle per call and are answered from a retained Java reference instead, three bake routes and two pipeline scene callbacks this renderer never enters, two initialisers that write zeroes a fresh Java array already has, one route that would make the game undestroyable (JAVA-UPSTREAM-011), cna_lod_group_ext_select which has no mesh part to return because this projection stores none, and cna_effect_get_image_based_light_ext, which ImageBasedLight answers from the textures it retained.
tasks.blocker: None, but most families need a real graphics device. The probe found that debug draw and the particle system both refuse an invalid one, so those tests have to run inside a Game, and anything whose result is a rendered image cannot be checked in a HEADLESS renderer at all -- which has to be stated rather than asserted around.
tasks.note: LodGroup deliberately holds thresholds rather than mesh parts: the Java projection's ModelMeshPart is a managed object with no native handle, so there is nothing to hand CNA and nothing meaningful to receive. selectIndex returns the level and the game draws what it keeps at that index. Five of DebugDraw's six gizmo routes are bound: the three light gizmos with the lighting slice, and the cluster-slice and cascade gizmos with the families whose handles they take. All six are bound now. cna_shadow_cascade_state_ext_init is deliberately unbound: no route in the whole C API consumes a CNA_ShadowCascadeStateEXT, so binding it would produce a value nothing can be handed to. Nothing in DebugDrawTests claims a line was drawn -- this qualification has a HEADLESS renderer -- only that the queue holds what was put in it, which is the part a game's own logic depends on. FrustumCuller is VERIFIED_PURE: it needs no device, and its evidence is agreement with XNA's own BoundingFrustum across a 125-box grid. Which XNA test matters -- CNA's culler is Contains(box) != Disjoint, the six-plane test, and XNA's Intersects is GJK. They disagree on boxes near a frustum corner, always with the plane test being the one that drops, and the projection measures that divergence rather than hiding it. The first version of the test used a camera at the origin looking down -Z, whose view matrix is the identity -- against which a planted view/projection swap passed. The camera is off-axis now. The two caster-effect accessors on each shadow map are deliberately unbound: applyCaster is the operation a game needs, and a borrowed engine effect has no Java facade with a coherent lifetime yet. The light-probe baker's thirteen routes are unbound: its three bake routes each take a scene-draw callback the generator refuses, and a baker that cannot bake reports only its own configuration. PostProcessChain and cna_post_process_pass_apply are unbound: their CNA_PostProcessContext carries a borrowed pointer to a CNA_RenderPipelineSettingsEXT, a struct field the generator refuses rather than guesses at, and the render pipeline runs the passes anyway. cna_render_pipeline_set_transparent_scene and _set_shadow_scene each take a draw callback the generator refuses; cna_render_pipeline_get_scene_target and _get_shadow_map return borrows with no release route and no documented lifetime, so a Java facade over either would be a dangling reference waiting to happen. PbrMaterialExtensions' nine texture getters are unbound with a reason: CNA mints a fresh borrowed handle on every call, which the caller must then release, so asking it for a texture the Java object already retains would allocate and free a native handle on every read and hand back a facade nobody owns. The transparent draw list is unbound: its submit route takes a draw callback the generator refuses, and a list nothing can be submitted to is not a feature. WeightedBlendedTransparency's two texture getters are unbound too -- CNA documents the borrow and not how it is given back, and a facade over a borrow with no stated release is a leak or a dangling reference depending on which guess is right. The environment processor's generate routes are NOT_SUPPORTED_BY_RENDERER except generateBrdfLut, which integrates rather than sampling a cube map and works here. cna_skybox_get_environment is unbound: CNA lends the cube map without saying how the borrow is given back, and the Java object retains what it was given instead.

tasks.title: Decide what RenderPipelineSettings projects, now that there are two of them
tasks.currentState: Decided and done. CNA's own header settles it: the frozen ten-field CNA_RenderPipelineSettings cannot grow inside an ABI major, so the complete shape arrived under a new name, and every engine-layer route that takes settings -- including the pipeline's own get and set -- takes the larger one. RenderPipelineSettingsExt projects it, with all fifty fields and CNA's own prose on each. RenderPipelineSettings keeps its name and its narrower job, because it is a faithful projection of a CNA type that still exists.
tasks.expectedState: Achieved. normalize() is the method that earns the type: CNA warns that writing a field is not the same as the engine storing it -- thirty-one of them correct their input -- and normalize asks what would actually be stored. applyFrom() applies serialized text and reports how many fields it recognised, which is what a console command or a config file wants.
tasks.blocker: None technically -- all three value routes plan cleanly. It needs the design call first, because growing a published type from 10 properties to 50 is not something to do by accident, and it decides whether the existing one keeps its name.
tasks.note: Found while looking for an engine-layer family that could be qualified with no renderer. The three settings value routes are exactly that -- pure functions on a structure -- and they were bound, then unbound again when the two structures turned out to be different. Binding them against the smaller Java type would have silently truncated forty fields.

It is recorded so the next reader does not spend the same hour, and so that a future CNA that changes the parameter to match its documentation is noticed rather than silently breaking every clustered call.

tasks.title: A documented INVALID_STATE refusal arrives as INTERNAL, because the exception barrier has no logic_error arm
tasks.currentState: Re-measured 2026-09-30 against CNA ABI 0.35.0 (next at 0f7166cd8/79799cf09; ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0 HEADLESS and ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0-opengles3-fx). No longer applicable: CNA ABI 0.30 removed engine_layer.h and every route this finding names; the Java families that bound them were deleted with it. The general barrier fix (BINDFIX-003) is in CNA.
tasks.expectedState: Either the barrier grows a std::logic_error arm mapping to INVALID_STATE, or the engine throws something the barrier already maps. Until then a game cannot tell a refusal it can act on -- turn the fallback on -- from a defect inside CNA, which is exactly the distinction CNA_RESULT_INTERNAL exists to make.
tasks.note: CNA-Java works around it soundly rather than by matching on the message: InstancedRenderer.draw asks the renderer its own two questions on the failure path only -- can it instance, is the fallback on -- and raises IllegalStateException when they explain the refusal, keeping CNA's failure and its real result code as the cause. The workaround costs nothing on the success path and stops working correctly the moment CNA fixes the result, at which point it simply becomes redundant rather than wrong. Likely wider than this one route: std::logic_error is thrown in more than one place in the engine layer.

tasks.title: A texture applied through a PBR material is invisible to the C API afterwards
tasks.currentState: Re-measured 2026-09-30 against CNA ABI 0.35.0 (next at 0f7166cd8/79799cf09; ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0 HEADLESS and ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0-opengles3-fx). No longer applicable: CNA ABI 0.30 removed engine_layer.h and every route this finding names; the Java families that bound them were deleted with it. cna_pbr_effect_set_texture/get_texture survive and PbrEffect uses them.
tasks.expectedState: apply_material records each slot's handle the way set_texture does, so that a material extracted from an effect names the textures the effect is actually using. Until then the read-modify-write a game naturally writes -- extract, change one number, apply -- silently unbinds every map, because the extracted material carries no textures to put back.
tasks.note: PbrEffect.applyMaterial works around it by setting each slot a second time through cna_pbr_effect_set_texture, so the registry agrees with the effect and a read-modify-write keeps its maps. That is additive rather than compensating: when CNA closes the gap the second pass becomes redundant rather than wrong, and the test -- which asserts the round trip keeps the texture -- keeps passing either way. The probe is what pins CNA's own behaviour, and it is where a fix would show up first.

tasks.title: Handing a pass to a post-process chain makes the game undestroyable
tasks.currentState: Re-measured 2026-09-30 against CNA ABI 0.35.0 (next at 0f7166cd8/79799cf09; ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0 HEADLESS and ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0-opengles3-fx). No longer applicable: CNA ABI 0.30 removed engine_layer.h and every route this finding names; the Java families that bound them were deleted with it.
tasks.expectedState: The route decrements the owned-child count as cna_post_process_pass_destroy does, so a game that hands a pass to a chain shuts down like any other. One hand-over anywhere in a game's lifetime is enough to break shutdown, which makes this the more severe of the two ownership findings.
tasks.note: The route is deliberately not bound. PostProcessChain is fully usable through add_pass, which borrows and leaves the caller closing its own passes -- an ordinary thing to ask -- so shipping a method that quietly makes shutdown impossible would be worse than the absence. Bind it when the accounting is fixed.

tasks.title: Project the handles the engine layer lends once their lifetimes are stated or measured
tasks.currentState: Done for twenty-two of the thirty-five routes, and every one of the fourteen that remain is unbound for a reason that is not a renderer. lent_effect_lifetime.c and lent_handle_use_after_lender.c measured each lender on four questions and found two opposite contracts hiding under one word. COUNTED borrows, whose lender refuses to be destroyed while one is out: three of the four shadow maps caster effects, the depth/normal prepass two, and the clustered forward effect shader. RETAINING borrows, which may outlive their lender: the spot map caster, the clustered effect own material extensions and the transparency resolve two targets. Nothing dangles -- every lender that permits its own destruction really is retained by what it lent. The render pipeline scene target is a third shape, valid only inside an open frame.
tasks.expectedState: Each lent handle projected as the facade its measured lifetime allows, rather than one guess applied to twenty.
tasks.note: The nine PbrMaterialExtensions texture getters are bound as hasClearcoatTexture and its eight siblings, and cna_effect_get_image_based_light_ext as EffectLighting.hasImageBasedLight -- a boolean with the fresh names given straight back, which is the treatment cna_effect_get_shadow_map_ext already had. That is what lets a material borrowed from an effect say what is bound, having been given nothing through Java, and it is the only way to ask an effect about its environment at all, because setImageBasedLight is a static call over textures the caller owns and nothing here retains them. The thirteen still unbound are redundant getters whose answer Java already holds (the pipeline shadow map and skybox, the skybox environment, the two colour-grade LUTs, the clustered effect opaque frame, the two glTF initialisers, the LOD group mesh-part select), a getter that leaks (the post-process effect pass effect), a pure value test (the memory-barrier containment), the ASCII pass effect -- a non-owning view cna_effect_destroy refuses, which no Java facade can own -- and the one route that makes a game undestroyable, JAVA-UPSTREAM-011.

tasks.title: Project automatic exposure when a renderer that can measure luminance can qualify it
tasks.currentState: Done. All thirteen routes are bound and reached as AutoExposure. The meter needs compute, which OPENGLES3 and OPENGL33 have, and the tests measure rather than assert existence: a grey of 8/255 and one of 240/255 come back as their own luminances, adaptation moves the exposure down for the brighter scene and up for the darker one, the key value doubles the exposure it asks for, and both clamping setters are asserted correcting what they were given. Three planted mutations registered.
tasks.expectedState: A measured average luminance, a key value, adaptation speeds and a clamp, all reachable at once on a renderer that can read a frame back -- and it is.
tasks.note: cna_auto_exposure_ext_apply_to needed the generator declared in/out shape -- a non-const CNA_RenderPipelineSettingsEXT the declaration does not mark as an output -- which routes.json now states. The test asserts the other side of that: applying the exposure leaves every other setting alone, which an output-only marshalling would have zeroed.

tasks.title: Project the compute family when a renderer that has compute can qualify it
tasks.currentState: Done. All twenty-six routes of the compute family are bound and reached: ComputeShader, StorageBuffer, ImageAccess, MemoryBarrier, IndirectDraw and the two indirect-argument value types. A renderer with compute exists on this host after all -- not the desktop GL 4.3 the previous handoff predicted, but CNA EasyGL family reached through OPENGLES3 (an OpenGL ES 3.2 context) and OPENGL33 (which asks Mesa for 3.3 core and is handed 4.6 or 4.5). The acceptance test is semantic rather than structural: four known integers into a storage buffer, a dispatch that doubles them and adds a uniform, a readback compared against the same arithmetic in Java. Five of six planted mutations registered.
tasks.expectedState: One coherent family a game can dispatch work with, and it is that.
tasks.note: cna_graphics_memory_barrier_has is the one route deliberately left unbound: it is a pure bitmask containment test over integers the caller supplies, which java.util.EnumSet answers for nothing, and it reveals nothing about CNA own bit values. Those are pinned in probe.c instead, where a compile-time assertion against the live header is stronger than any runtime route could be.

tasks.title: A compute shader that does not compile is reported as an internal failure rather than as a shader carrying a compile error
tasks.currentState: Re-measured 2026-09-30 against CNA ABI 0.35.0 (next at 0f7166cd8/79799cf09; ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0 HEADLESS and ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0-opengles3-fx). No longer applicable: CNA ABI 0.30 removed engine_layer.h and every route this finding names; the Java families that bound them were deleted with it.
tasks.expectedState: Creation succeeds and the failure is read off the object, as the header says -- which would make the two documented routes reachable for the case they exist for.
tasks.note: Two consequences. cna_compute_shader_is_valid and cna_compute_shader_copy_compile_error cannot answer the question they exist for, because a failed compile leaves no handle to ask. And the one refusal a game can act on -- a typo in a shader -- arrives as the result code that also means a defect inside CNA. The compiler own diagnostics do survive, in the barrier last message, which is what makes ComputeShader.compile able to throw a ShaderCompilationException carrying the GLSL log. That Java layer still asks isValid() on the success path, so the day CNA matches its header nothing here changes.

tasks.title: A process exiting with a live vertex buffer aborts on the EasyGL renderer
tasks.currentState: Re-measured 2026-09-30 against CNA ABI 0.35.0 (next at 0f7166cd8/79799cf09; ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0 HEADLESS and ~/deps/cna-c-abi-0.35.0-opengles3-fx). A game that closes its buffers is unaffected; one that calls System.exit, or dies on an unhandled exception, is not. The subprocess test asserts the abort exact signature on the renderers where it is known, so an upstream fix shows up as a failing test.

tasks.title: Creating a graphics device resets three renderer-selection query routes, and three more named "current" report the compile-time default

tasks.title: Project CNA's renderer selection so a game can ask what this build has before it asks for one
tasks.currentState: GraphicsRenderer, GraphicsRendererType and GraphicsRendererFallback project eighteen of the family's twenty-two routes: the inventory, per-identity availability, per-identity category and maturity, case-insensitive name parsing, the preference setters, the fallback chain with its history and CNA's own messages and reason names, the active renderer, and the test-only reset. The three routes a device resets are not bound (JAVA-UPSTREAM-018), and the two current-name routes were already bound.
tasks.expectedState: A game reads GraphicsRenderer.available(), decides, and calls setPreferred -- rather than exporting CNA_GRAPHICS_RENDERER and finding out at load time that the renderer is not there (JAVA-UPSTREAM-017).
tasks.note: Falsified with three planted defects, all of which failed the suite: a wrong CNA number on one identity (6 of 9 tests), parse() ignoring whether CNA recognised the name (1), and a refused selection treated as an accepted one (2). This projection had been reading the renderer inventory out of CMakeCache.txt; the routes to ask the library were there the whole time. Binding the per-identity classifiers is what exposed the current-route half of JAVA-UPSTREAM-018 -- a test written to check two routes agreed found that they did not.

tasks.title: ColorGradePass bound its volume table to the wrong texture type, and nothing had ever tested it
tasks.currentState: setVolumeLut and getVolumeLut take and return a Texture3D. CNA documents the argument as "a cube with an edge between two and CNA_COLOR_GRADE_MAX_LUT_SIZE_EXT", which reads two ways; measured, a TextureCube is refused with INVALID_HANDLE and a cubical Texture3D is accepted. Java validates the same shape CNA does -- cubical, edge 2 to 64 -- and names the shape it was given rather than forwarding a result code.
tasks.expectedState: A game can bind a volume grading table, which it could not before: the previous signature took a TextureCube and could never have succeeded.
tasks.note: The signature was wrong and untested at the same time, which is the only way a signature this wrong survives: no test had ever bound a volume table, so there was nothing for the error to fail against. Found by a probe that bound one to ask a lifetime question about the getter. The first falsification attempt did not register -- asserting only the exception type passed with the Java validation deleted, because CNA raises the same type -- so the assertions read the message, which is what the Java check actually adds.
